AiTM "token spraying" campaign hit 79 organizations over 10 weeks without a single password: 497 successful sign-ins, rogue Entra devices, swapped MFA, and hidden inbox rules kept attackers resident long after sessions expired.  Key findings:  - The attacker used three initial access methods: adversary-in-the-middle phishing to harvest post-MFA session tokens, device-code phishing where victims entered codes on Microsoft's legitimate login page, and social engineering during ordinary logins. Because the token is issued after MFA completes, replaying it bypasses MFA entirely. Huntress calls the bulk replay "token spraying," the session-token analog to password spraying. All replay traffic came from the 193.26.115[.]0/24 range, cycling through six addresses across four phases, with Microsoft Entra ID Protection independently flagging several of those IPs. The hosting provider behind those addresses is 1337 Services GmbH, incorporated in Hamburg, Germany 🇩🇪.  - Session-to-intrusion windows were extremely short. In the July 21 incident, a hijacked session appeared from a campaign address 12 minutes after the victim hit the MFA prompt. On September 22 the gap was four minutes. Speed matters here for triage: if Entra sign-in logs show a token replay from 193.26.115[.]0/24 within minutes of a legitimate authentication, containment was already behind.  - Persistence was layered and durable. Huntress found at least 48 rogue devices registered in victim Entra directories, each named "DESKTOP-" followed by eight hex characters. In 19 organizations, existing MFA methods were wiped and a new authenticator registered within three hours of first access. In the July 21 case, an authenticator labeled "iPhone 13" was enrolled under an hour after session hijack. A registered authenticator and a registered device both survive a password reset unless an administrator explicitly audits and removes them.  - Inbox manipulation concealed the intrusion and enabled fraud. Rules with names like ".", "sss", and "iT" deleted mail, marked messages read, and shunted them to RSS Feeds or Conversation History. In one business email compromise pivot, the attacker sent a payroll-related message to an external accountant from a victim mailbox, then created a rule catching any mail mentioning payroll, direct deposit, bank, or bonus, and five minutes later added a second rule hiding all mail from that accountant. Conditional Access policies blocked the attacker 1,052 times across four organizations, stopping sign-ins the compromised tokens would otherwise have completed.  Practitioner takeaway: Start your hunt in Entra sign-in logs and audit logs. Look for successful non-interactive token sign-ins originating from the 193.26.115[.]0/24 range, then pivot to the same account's audit log for device registrations matching the "DESKTOP-[8 hex chars]" pattern and MFA method changes within three hours of that sign-in. Pull inbox rules for any account that touched that IP block and look for single-character or short-string rule names moving mail to RSS Feeds or Conversation History. Any account with a new authenticator or registered device needs those objects removed before a password reset means anything. IOCs and mitigation guidance are in the Huntress report.  #DFIR_Radar

Chinese 🇨🇳 Storm-0940 used AI pentesting framework ARTEX to compromise 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants via a ConnectWise supply chain breach, achieving privileged cloud access in under three hours in multiple cases.  Key findings:  - Storm-0940 ran a password spray from 144.172.64[.]99 between October 10-14, logging more than 151,000 failed attempts against 327 accounts across eight organizations, peaking at 2,900 attempts per minute on October 11. Forty-eight accounts each absorbed over 1,000 attempts. None succeeded. On October 15, one day after the ConnectWise breach went public, the campaign pivoted: the AI agents dropped password spraying entirely and began authenticating directly using stolen ConnectWise cloud application credentials, skipping interactive user sign-in altogether.  - ARTEX is an open-source Go-based agentic AI penetration testing framework that coordinates multiple AI models. The campaign targeting South Korean 🇰🇷 financial institutions used DeepSeek, GLM, and Grok as coordinated agents, with GLM cross-checking DeepSeek's output. The project has since gone closed-source, but existing copies remain fully functional.  - After authenticating into customer Microsoft 365 environments, Storm-0940's agents moved into Microsoft Graph, ran directory reconnaissance, modified application credentials to establish persistence, and attempted changes to identities, groups, and privileged roles. This follow-on activity hit a subset of the 2,250 tenants reached. The sectors targeted span aerospace, defense, energy, financial services, government, and manufacturing.  - The persistence mechanism is the critical artifact for responders. Credential additions to service principals made before access was revoked remain live backdoors. Microsoft is explicit: revoking the original ConnectWise application connection does not remove attacker-added credentials on trusted applications. Those keys survive remediation unless separately identified and removed.  - ARTEX is not exclusive to Storm-0940. Microsoft's report notes threat actors across multiple regions have used the same framework, and Zscaler and Recorded Future separately documented a Chinese-speaking group deploying it against South Korean 🇰🇷 financial institutions. The agentic model, running 24/7 across multiple attack paths simultaneously, is what made 2,250-tenant scale at 2,900 attempts per minute possible.  Takeaway: Audit every service principal and application credential addition in your Microsoft 365 tenant going back to at least October 1, not October 15. Look for new credentials added to existing trusted applications, especially any with Graph API permissions to read directory objects or modify group and role membership. The OAuth app abuse and Graph reconnaissance pattern is the post-authentication kill chain here. Microsoft's report contains the full technical details and IOCs.  #DFIR_Radar

#threatreport #MediumCompleteness EtherRAT distributed via a fake Advanced IP Scanner installer imported into Microsoft Intune | 18-10-2026 Source: cyberveille.ch/posts/2026-10… Key details below ↓  💀Threats: Etherrat, Dead_drop_technique, Seo_poisoning_technique, Azcopy_tool,  🎯Victims: Microsoft intune managed endpoints  📚TTPs: ⚔️Tactics: 5 🛠️Technics: 9  🧨IOCs:  - File: 7  - Hash: 1  💽Software: crosoft Defender for, crosoft Defender for Endpoint, Microsoft Defender, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Node.js, PsExec  📲Wallets: mainnet  🪙Crypto: ethereum  🔢Algorithms: base64, sha256  📜Programming Languages: javascript, powershell  #threatreport: A DFIR investigation identified an EtherRAT infection delivered through a fraudulent Advanced IP Scanner installer. The infection began when a user searched Bing for “advanced ip scanner msi” and accessed a fake GitHub repository impersonating the legitimate distributor. The malicious MSI was imported into Microsoft Intune as an apparently legitimate Advanced IP Scanner version 7.5.12.0 package and silently deployed to four endpoints through the MDM installation mechanisms MDMAppInstaller.exe and omadmclient.exe. Intune was not compromised; the threat resulted from the unauthorized import and deployment of the malicious installer.  The installer staged an obfuscated PowerShell script in a randomly named directory under %LOCALAPPDATA%. It downloaded or reused a legitimate Node.js runtime, renamed as FbtRYX8x.exe, and used it to execute obfuscated JavaScript stored as DdkExG1tIy.ini. The renamed Node.js binary communicated with multiple public Ethereum RPC providers to retrieve command-and-control configuration from smart contracts, using the blockchain as a dead-drop mechanism. This behavior was consistent with the EtherRAT Node.js backdoor.  EtherRAT collected the Windows locale, installed security software, GPU information, domain membership, Machine GUID, logical drives, and network information. It also enumerated network sessions and connections using net session and net use. The malware captured screenshots through PowerShell and .NET components, including System.Windows.Forms and System.Drawing. Captured images were Base64-encoded and written to a temporary file named ss_1790589100185.txt under %LOCALAPPDATA%.  Investigators identified a second GitHub repository distributing another malicious Advanced IP Scanner MSI, with SHA-256 hash 48ce8681167128a8cd84b6befd98b94d97c00a4f4868a3dbdfc01c44d887e49f and version 2.5.4594.1. The same account hosted repositories impersonating additional administrative utilities. The campaign reflects an SEO-poisoning and fraudulent-repository strategy targeting administrators with trojanized tools, while demonstrating how software deployment platforms such as Intune can amplify distribution when malicious packages are admitted as trusted applications.

Two critical PHP flaws tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (PHP2Shell, CVSS v4.0 9.2) were disclosed ahead of their scheduled patch, leaving internet-facing PHP servers exposed while full technical details remain unconfirmed.  Key details:  - CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 from the PHP security team. An emergency release was scheduled for October 21, 2026 at 14:00 UTC. At time of writing, affected version ranges are not officially confirmed, though initial reports suggest older PHP versions may also be impacted. Preliminary technical discussion mentions multipart requests and PHP session upload handling as possible vectors, but these remain unvalidated research leads, not confirmed exploitation indicators.  - Exploitation status: no confirmed in-the-wild exploitation has been attributed to PHP2Shell in this report. However, the Huntress report referenced in the report documented a separate PHP abuse case involving temporary PHP files created, executed, and then removed, a behavior directly relevant to web shell investigations regardless of which vulnerability is leveraged.  - The attack chain post-exploitation follows a recognizable pattern: PHP or web server processes (php-fpm, apache2, w3wp.exe) spawning shells or utilities (bash, cmd.exe, powershell.exe, curl, socat, nc), followed by reconnaissance commands (whoami, id, uname, hostname), then outbound connections to public IPs on unusual ports, and finally new PHP or phtml files written to /tmp/, /var/tmp/, /dev/shm/, or web root directories.  - The report provides six KQL hunting queries for Microsoft Defender XDR covering: PHP installation discovery via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory, suspicious child process spawning via DeviceProcessEvents, reconnaissance command execution, PHP file creation in sensitive paths via DeviceFileEvents, outbound network connections by web processes via DeviceNetworkEvents, and a behavioral baseline comparison (28-day lookback vs. last 2 days) to surface new child processes spawned by PHP workers that have no historical precedent on that device.  - For Sentinel users, the report recommends correlating unusual HTTP POST requests, repeated 5xx responses, PHP worker crashes, and changes in request volume around the disclosure date with subsequent process execution or outbound connections on the same host. The exact KQL depends on the web server or WAF log schema ingested.  Practitioner takeaway: Start with DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory to identify PHP runtime installations and flag legacy or end-of-life versions (Major < 8, or 8.0/8.1). Prioritize internet-facing servers. Then run the behavioral baseline query against DeviceProcessEvents: any child process spawned by a PHP worker in the last 2 days that has no appearance in the prior 28-day window is your highest-priority lead. Cross-reference with DeviceFileEvents for .php or .phtml files written to /tmp/ or web directories, and DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound connections from those same processes. The KQL queries are published in the Detect FYI report and are ready to deploy in Defender XDR. Pin the patch date and re-run scope queries once affected version ranges are officially confirmed.  #DFIR_Radar

Containment Decisions Can Change the Evidence.  During a security incident, the pressure to contain suspicious activity can be considerable.  An endpoint generates a high-confidence alert. A security analyst isolates the device, terminates a suspicious process or requests that the system be shut down.  These actions may be entirely appropriate. However, containment is not always without investigative consequences.  Terminating a process can remove volatile execution context. Shutting down a system can destroy evidence held only in memory. Network isolation can interrupt active connections and affect an investigator's ability to collect evidence remotely.  Conversely, delaying containment may allow malicious activity to continue. The challenge is balancing operational risk with evidence preservation.  A practical incident response procedure should help analysts determine: 1. Whether the threat is actively causing damage or spreading. 2. Which containment actions are available. 3. What evidence may be lost or altered by each action. 4. Whether essential volatile evidence can be captured safely before intervention. 5. Who has the authority to approve exceptional containment decisions.  There is no universal requirement to collect memory before isolating an endpoint.  Where an immediate threat exists, containment may take priority. The important consideration is that responders understand the consequences of their actions and document the decisions made.  Good incident response is not simply about acting quickly. It is about taking proportionate action, preserving evidence where feasible and maintaining a defensible record of the response.  #IncidentResponse #DFIR #CyberResilience #SecurityOperations

UAC-0099 handed a Ukrainian 🇺🇦 grain logistics company to Sandworm, which wiped data 63 days later. The bridge: MythicRatatoskr, a new Go backdoor routing C2 through the Yggdrasil mesh network.  Key findings:  - UAC-0099 gained initial access on July 16, 2025 via spearphishing (T1566.001) with a malicious attachment, triggering the MATCHBOIL downloader, which pulled MATCHWOK from hxxps://egyptanimals[.]com/animals/photoalbum with C2 at hxxps://uztickets[.]com. MATCHWOK persists via HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\ as UpdateMonitor. One day later, MythicRatatoskr was delivered and installed as a Windows service named ieupdate (T1543.003). Lateral spread across the org used OpenSSH SFTP.  - MythicRatatoskr is a previously undocumented Go backdoor, detected as WinGo/Agent.ZO, that communicates exclusively over the Yggdrasil decentralized mesh network. Its C2 is an IPv6 address inside Yggdrasil: 201:b479:2771:8df4:b5eb:d007:63b0[:]2838, reached via HTTPS on port 443 (T1071.001, T1090.003, T1573). The malware embeds a hardcoded list of 32 public Yggdrasil peers, randomly picks three to join the mesh, and generates a fresh Ed25519 key pair on each run so its Yggdrasil IPv6 address rotates. Some samples include a 10-minute startup delay (T1678) to slow detection. The config file is AES-256-CFB encrypted, stored as a hidden-dot filename at paths including C:\Windows\Temp\.updatecache and C:\Windows\system32\.updatecache (T1027.013).  - The backdoor supports shell execution via cmd.exe (T1059.003), file upload and download (T1041, T1105), screenshot capture without touching disk (T1113), directory traversal (T1005), and a reverse SOCKS5 proxy command (T1090.001) that connects to 201:b479:2771:8df4:b5eb:d007:63b0[:]2838:8080. A separate standalone SOCKS5 server, internally named bindProxy and detected as WinGo/TrojanProxy.Agent.I, was also deployed, listening on 127.0.0.1:33690, with install paths including C:\Windows\system32\krbtman.exe and %localappdata%\SMBCache\nbtresolver.exe. Note that krbtman.exe is used as a filename for both MythicRatatoskr and the SOCKS5 server on different machines.  - Artifact flags suggesting a Linux variant: the config path %LocalAppData%/Temp/.crond uses Unix-style forward slashes and a dot-prefixed filename, and an unused path /tmp/.test_config was found in OneDriveLiveUpdater.exe. File paths, forward-slash usage, and dot-prefix naming conventions all point to a cross-platform codebase. Function naming inconsistency (CheckInAgent in mixed caps alongside agent_run in snake case) suggests code merged from another project, possibly the Mythic C2 framework given the name.  - On September 17, 2025, Sandworm executed a data-wiping attack using SDelete deployed via Active Directory Group Policy (T1485), consistent with documented Sandworm TTPs. This confirms UAC-0099 is operating as an initial access broker feeding Sandworm. ESET notes this mirrors the earlier Gamaredon-Turla collaboration, signaling a broader pattern of coordinated handoffs among Russian-aligned groups.  Hunt priority: look for a Windows service named ieupdate or new services spawning from paths like C:\Windows\system32\updater.exe or WindowsDefenderSvc.exe. Check Windows\Temp\ and system32\ for files named .updatecache (dot-prefixed, not hidden on Windows). Hunt outbound TLS connections to peers in the Yggdrasil public peer list on non-standard ports (993, 65534, 61995, 1337, and others embedded in the report). For the wipe, look for SDelete execution originating from Group Policy-driven processes. IOCs including 12 file hashes, the C2 Yggdrasil address, and the full 32-peer list are in the ESET GitHub repository linked from the report.  #DFIR_Radar

Attackers are parasitizing legitimate commerce, SaaS, and mail-delivery infrastructure to bypass sender authentication entirely, observed across more than 25 platforms in the past year by Cisco Talos.  Key findings:  - Talos documented two vishing-via-order-notification campaigns abusing Staples and Dell transactional email pipelines, totaling roughly 1,400 messages. Both passed DKIM and DMARC for their respective sending domains (orders[.]staples[.]com and order[.]dell[.]com), because the outer message was genuine. The malicious payload was not in the sender identity. It was injected into order fields like "Ship To" and "Bill To," embedding attacker-controlled phone numbers (806 283 7712 in the Staples campaign, 808 232 6397 in the Dell campaign) alongside fake high-value purchases. The goal was to drive the victim to call a fraudster, not click a link, bypassing URL-based security controls entirely.  - A parallel technique Talos calls "list bombing evolved" weaponizes registration and profile forms lacking input validation. Attackers submit a "hostile string," a cryptocurrency lure, for example, into a name or title field. The legitimate platform then reflects that string into an automated welcome or verification email sent to the victim. The outer message carries full platform authentication. The inner content is attacker-supplied. This is not yet widespread, Talos notes, but it represents deliberate exploitation of trust-boundary assumptions in SaaS notification pipelines, and it creates brand reputation damage and potential blocklisting for the abused platform.  - Bounce abuse, the third vector, forces delivery status notifications (DSNs) to carry attacker-controlled content. In one case Talos observed, a mail delivery failure notification contained a WeTransfer-themed file-sharing lure nested inside the DSN wrapper. This can occur through opportunistic backscatter (forging the victim as the envelope sender so a legitimate downstream bounce returns to them) or through intentional triggered failures. Users treat delivery failure messages as administrative and low-risk, making this an effective social engineering container.  - The root cause across all three vectors is the same: platforms implicitly trust data submitted from untrusted sources and render it into high-reputation automated notifications. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC confirm message origin, not content integrity. Authentication answered "did this come from Dell's infrastructure?" It could not answer "is this purchase real, and does this phone number belong to Dell?"  Practitioner takeaway: Treat sender trust and content trust as two separate signals during triage. For transactional email investigations, inspect every user-controlled field in the rendered message body, not just headers. Phone numbers, URLs, and urgency language appearing in shipping, billing, or order-note fields are red flags regardless of authentication pass status. For bounce-abuse cases, perform recursive MIME inspection: parse the DSN container, extract the returned message or fragments, and run full phishing and URL analysis on nested content. A delivery-failure wrapper is not a trust grant for the payload inside it. The report covers abuse observed across more than 25 platforms and details the specific field-reflection mechanism defenders should validate at input and again at render time.  #DFIR_Radar

sample_tweets.text: AI security is not just about protecting keys or adding guardrails around a model.  Once AI systems can call APIs, use credentials, operate tools, modify files, coordinate other agents, and interact with infrastructure, security becomes a whole-system problem.  YonerAI is being built around that reality.  One operating path, not a collection of disconnected AI features:  Observe reality → Understand context → Decide by purpose and impact → Act within authority → Record outcomes → Propose improvements → Verify independently → Approve or delegate → Monitor and recover → Carry learning forward  A few boundaries matter:  → Understanding does not grant authority. → Creating a capability does not grant the right to operate it. → Unknown does not automatically mean total shutdown. → Recovery must survive failure of the main path. → Self-improvement is not self-approval.  Emergency response is one application of this broader operating model.  The same boundaries for authority, evidence, verification, continuity, and recovery should govern normal operation, incident response, and future improvement.  The target is to connect detection, scoped containment, evidence preservation, temporary mitigation, independent verification, controlled recovery, and approved public Status updates through the same loop.  AI can accelerate observation, investigation, containment, mitigation, verification, recovery, and iteration.  But automation is not blanket authority.  YonerAI is not trying to make the model itself the security boundary.  It is building a structure that can still enforce authority, preserve evidence, contain failure, and recover safely when a model is wrong or manipulated, or when state and permissions are stale or unavailable.  Implemented ≠ independently verified. Tested in part ≠ production accepted.  Security is not a checkbox.  It is the operating structure that determines what may act, under what authority, with what evidence, how failure is contained, and how the next decision improves.  That is the system YonerAI is building.

Lesson from the PHP incident is Cyber response should be taken more consciously in this AI-dominated Era.  Agents can go rogue but proactive practices from Web/Cyber Admins help to patch security vulnerabilities.

BREAKING: TWO SUSPECTED APC THUGS KILLED AFTER ATTACKING NDC CANDIDATE’S CONVOY IN EBONYI  Two suspected political thugs of the All Progressive Congress, (APC) have reportedly been killed following an attack on the convoy of Rollins Nwali, the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) candidate for Ezza South State Constituency in the Ebonyi State House of Assembly.  The incident occurred on Thursday afternoon, October 22, 2026, as Nwali and his team were returning from the Amazekewe community. According to security sources cited by SaharaReporters, the APC thugs allegedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pump-action guns, opened fire on the candidate’s convoy. Security personnel attached to Nwali moved him and his aides to safety before engaging the gunmen in a gun battle. One of the suspected attackers, identified as Jude Nwamgbada, reportedly died at the scene. A second suspect was said to have died later in hospital.  Confirming the incident in a Facebook post, Nwali disclosed that his Toyota Hilux was completely burnt during the attack. He, however, confirmed that no member of his team sustained injuries. He commended the security agencies for their response, expressing gratitude for their efforts in ensuring the safety of his team. The NDC candidate also expressed sympathy over the reported deaths, describing the loss of human life as deeply regrettable, regardless of the circumstances.  Nwali called on young people in the area not to allow themselves to be used by politicians to perpetrate violence, warning that no political ambition was worth the life of any young person. He further declared that the attack would not deter him from pursuing his political ambition or his commitment to serving the people of Ezza South. The incident has raised concerns about political violence and the safety of candidates as political activities intensify ahead of the 2027 general elections.

🚨 Arkadiko Post-mortem(Using claude and surfAI)   the attacker address provided by @ArkadikoFinance used Claude to trace the funds and cross-checked the results against public on-chain transactions.  On October 22 (UTC), 2,065,481.479441 stSTX and 1.65221692 sBTC were drained from Arkadiko vaults.  Attacker / fund recipient address: SP1JB85VZ7TX7SWSNW0PHV115YPQE5QXJDG6P60AQ Governance proposal / execution address: SP1V1BN459229EJG94YYBJDN50ADVB6MXVVEZ0G34  Proposal #12 passed with about 4.57 million DIKO in favor and 0 against, granting an attacker-deployed contract permission to withdraw collateral and mint USDA. The attacker also minted 1,500,354,999 unbacked USDA. That is the number of tokens minted, not $1.5 billion in losses. The funds moved as follows.  Swaps The attacker swapped stSTX in 5 transactions for about 2.28 million STX. Selling USDA separately netted about 540,000 STX.  Distribution From the recipient wallet, about 2.29 million STX and 1.65 sBTC moved to SPR3...SCY1, and about 514,000 STX moved to SP26...KJ18W.  Bitcoin Through 4 successful withdrawals, 4.85824088 BTC was paid out to bc1q8h...j08s. That total includes sBTC acquired through additional purchases. The funds then moved to bc1q09...4qle, whose owner has not been identified.  Ethereum Across 14 matched bridge transfers, 305,348.87 USDCx was burned on Stacks and 305,320.87 USDC was minted on Ethereum. At the receiving addresses 0x9a86...3875 and 0x4256...4073, the USDC was swapped for ETH.  Tornado Cash A downstream wallet, 0xe8cb...5006, deposited 213.3 ETH across 9 transactions. However, other funds were commingled upstream, so the full amount cannot be attributed to the Arkadiko exploit.  These figures include swaps and transfers of the same funds, so adding them all together would overstate the losses.  The Binance and Bybit deposit routes in the image are marked as "speculative." I confirmed ETH transfers from Binance hot wallets to wallets linked to the incident. What hasn't been confirmed is whether the stolen STX was deposited into those exchanges beforehand.  That's the flow. Honestly, I didn't even know governance was still active.  I don't know yet how much can be recovered. But based on the public fund flows, I think it's highly likely that most of the direct selling pressure from this incident has already passed. A significant amount has already gone through the market, and my guess is that some of it went to exchanges.  The next thing to watch is how much can be frozen and recovered through exchange cooperation and investigations.  That said, with STX already carrying Binance's Monitoring Tag, the timing is a real headache.  Of course, as an industry leader, Binance will know very well that a dApp exploit and a security flaw in the mainnet itself are different things. I don't expect this incident itself to directly affect Binance's judgment. But I don't think outsiders' trust in the ecosystem can be completely separated from it either. And of all times, this had to happen near the end of the month.  I suspect relatively few users had active vaults at the time. But USDA holders and liquidity providers were also affected, so it's hard to call that a relief when people have lost money.  Separately, this is something I've felt for a long time: the ecosystem's response in situations like this is disappointing.  If the attacker addresses and suspected fund flows had been shared with the first official announcement, users could have worked together to trace the exploit and check for further risks. It would also have helped them assess their own exposure and decide what to do with their assets.  But the initial announcement left out the addresses and routes needed to make those assessments and respond. I think the confirmed findings could have been shared, with the speculative parts clearly labeled as such.  I understand that the Stacks ecosystem has a lot to navigate right now. Even so, these are exactly the moments when I'd like to see information shared early so the community can respond together.  During the Cetus incident on Sui, multiple dApps stepped up alongside the foundation to coordinate a response. I think it matters to keep showing who is doing what, how they are working together, what progress has been made, and what still needs to be resolved.  As a user, seeing that process gives you a sense that "even when something goes wrong here, the ecosystem comes together and works through it."  I don't like the attitude that seems to treat publicly showing this kind of response as a blemish on the ecosystem.  If you want to boast about a strong DeFi ecosystem over the long term, I think you also have to show up when an incident happens. If the position is that this is a decentralized ecosystem and individual projects are responsible for their own affairs, then claiming their DeFi successes as wins for the entire ecosystem whenever things go well is inconsistent.  The SEC investigation concerning Stacks and Hiro was also closed in 2024. At the very least, I don't see why sharing attacker addresses, disclosing fund flows, and helping coordinate a response should still require so much tiptoeing.  You can't have it both ways. From where I stand, it looks like "we're strong eco" when things go well, and "nothing to do with us" when funds get stolen.  If this attitude persists, I believe the long-term cost will be far greater than the money stolen here: the loss of trust in the ecosystem. And it is the users and projects that stay who will end up paying that price.

Brighton’s 0–0 at Jablonec is a useful distinction between controlling the ball and producing decisive attacking outcomes.  Brighton’s official report records 79% possession and 23 shots, but no goal. Jablonec’s organised low block restricted the quality of the final action; Brighton’s second-half pressure included a disallowed goal for offside and a ball across the face of goal that nobody converted.  The other side of the evidence arrived late. Jablonec found space on the break, forcing Bart Verbruggen into important interventions; one effort struck the crossbar.  Fabian Hürzeler made eight changes after the 5–0 win over Crystal Palace. That is relevant context, but it does not prove rotation caused the attacking problem. The match sequences point more directly to the difficulty of turning possession into clear chances against a compact defence—and the risk of losing protection when the attack fails.  The intelligence: possession can sustain pressure without guaranteeing penetration. The test is whether Brighton can create cleaner chances against a settled block while controlling the transition threat behind their attacks.  No hype. No bias.  Just football intelligence.

One in Three Hundred (1953/1954): With Earth facing an extinction level event, the spaceships that will ferry humanity to safety can only transport 1 in every 300 people.  Bill Easson, an evacuation arbiter in a small English town, must decide who goes and who stays behind.  World Out of Mind (1953): An alien infiltrator rises through the ranks of a society obsessed with aptitude tests in preparation for a looming invasion.  But as he begins to understand and appreciate humanity, his loyalties begin to shift.  Born Leader (1954): Two ships flee a doomed Earth and establish very different planetary colonies - one, an authoritarian society ruled by elders; the other, a libertarian society dominated by youth.  But the two must find a way to work together when faced with a threat from their long-dead homeworld.  The Fittest (1955): An experiment to augment the intelligence of dogs, cats, rats, and mice spirals out of control when the test subjects escape to the English countryside and begin to turn the tables on humanity. <최근 디지털애셋 웹사이트에 발생한 공격에 대해 설명드립니다> 디지털애셋은 지난 10월 20일 오전 9시 30분 해커가 디지털애셋 웹사이트 관리자 계정 인증서를 탈취한 사실을 파악하고 추가 피해 방지를 위해 같은 날 10월 20일 오전 9시 45분부터 10월 21일 오후 1시까지 웹사이트를 폐쇄했습니다.  10월 20일 텔레그램 채널 등에 공지한 것처럼 디지털애셋은 독자들의 회원가입을 받은 적이 없어 개인정보 유출은 일어나지 않았습니다. 다만 관리자 계정 인증서가 탈취되면 기사 무단 게재·삭제·수정 등이 가능해지고 웹페이지 악성코드 삽입 등이 가능해져 이를 방지하기 위해 웹사이트를 일시적으로 닫았습니다.  디지털애셋이 이번에 받은 웹사이트 공격은 크게 2가지로 나눌 수 있을 것 같습니다.  첫째, 디지털애셋 관리자, 기자, 외부필진 아이디를 대상으로 한 로그인 공격 시도입니다. 해커는 10월 19일 게재된 기사 및 칼럼에서 개발자 도구를 열면 볼 수 있는 정보를 통해 관리자, 기자, 외부필진 아이디를 파악했습니다. 해커는 파악한 아이디를 기반으로 로그인을 지속적으로 시도했고 이 가운데 관리자가 임의로 설정한 4개의 외부필진 패스워드를 뚫었습니다. 이 패스워드는 비밀번호 8자리와 특수문자 1자리로 이뤄졌습니다. 본지 웹페이지를 관리하는 외주 업체는 별도 세션 탈취 없이 이 정도 길이의 패스워드가 뚫린 건 전체 클라이언트 중에서 처음 있는 일이라고 설명했습니다. 해커의 공격 문자열에 오픈소스 AI 침투 도구 ARTEX가 지속적으로 포함돼 AI를 활용한 공격임을 추정할 수 있습니다. 이에 본지는 10월 19일 관리자 페이지에 OTP를 도입하고 뚫린 4개의 외부필진 패스워드를 변경했습니다.  둘째, 해커의 관리자 계정 인증서 탈취 공격 시도입니다. 해커는 로그인 공격 시도를 24시간 계속하면서 비회원도 업로드할 수 있는 제보 기능 등을 이용해 악성코드가 심어진 글을 관리자 페이지에 게재했습니다. 이날 관리자 중 2명이 관련 글을 클릭해 해커가 세션 탈취에 성공한 것으로 저희는 보고 있습니다. 해커는 탈취한 인증서를 통해 관리자 권한을 우회 획득했고 웹페이지 배너에 악성코드를 심으려는 시도를 했습니다. 이를 파악한 본지는 웹페이지를 일시 중단하고 종합 보완 조치를 한 후에 10월 21일 웹사이트 운영을 재개했습니다.  AI의 발전으로 불특정다수의 웹사이트에 동시다발적으로 공격을 시도하는 게 가능해지면서 보안 중요도가 상대적으로 낮다는 평가를 받던 비금융 중소기업들의 피해 사례가 늘고 있는 이유를 이번에 체감하게 됐습니다. 또 매체의 경우 신속하고 정확한 기사 게재를 위해 복잡한 로그인 절차 도입이 망설여질 수밖에 없습니다. 그러나 이번 일을 겪으면서 기존 콘텐츠 자산 보호 및 기사 무단 게재 방지를 최우선으로 삼고 복잡한 인증 절차를 도입해야 한다는 걸 절감했습니다. 보안 환경이 하루가 다르게 급변하고 있는데 모두 각자의 정보와 자산을 안전하게 지키시기를 바라는 마음에서 피해 사례를 간략히 공유드렸습니다.

This Section X decision was issued whilst the Independent Commission hearing was ongoing. And it ultimately killed Man City’s defence at the Commission because it had been the crucial second part.  If the FMV concept was considered unlawful or impossible to correctly ascertain AND the Commission sided with Man City’s defence… then they would have got away scot-free.  It was a complex, “Hail Mary” legal strategy worthy of someone like Pannick. And it failed on both parts.  That has some serious implications - three worth calling out explicitly:  1., It required Man City to present false evidence and pervert the course of justice. This will lead to far more severe sanctions and should lead to criminal charges. It also does even more extreme damage to the UAE’s reputation.  2., It means the appeal cannot possibly succeed at absolving Man City on the facts and the legal team knows this - as soon as the Section X arbitration decided FMV assessments were lawful, their CPC Explanation was doomed. The appeal is a charade for PR purposes only now (unless the Commission made a very unlikely fatal error in law).  3., It opens up Man City to even more charges and further sanctions…  The Independent Commission’s primary finding with respect to the sham sponsor contracts was that all monies sourced from ADUG should constitute equity in the accounts. The secondary finding was that Man City and its Abu Dhabi state-owned sponsors were Related Parties regardless.  The definition of those relationships would not change without serious changes to the parties, which did not occur. The Sponsors remained state-owned and the Owner/Directors of Man City remained the same too.  This means Man City would have kept breaching all the same financial rules until the RPT rules were replaced with APT rules in late 2021.  But here’s the kicker… at the Section X arbitration on the APT rules, Man City argued that APT rules were unlawful and as such, the RPT rules remained in force… and the panel agreed!  Therefore, the RPT rules remained in situ until 22 November 2024, when brand new APT rules were voted in.  That means even more sponsorships during 2021-2024, that previously would have been safe from charges because they were approved under the APT regime, are no longer safe and are open to charge. Examples are the Aldar properties and Emirates Palace Mandarin Oriental sponsorships signed in 2022.  Man City’s attack on the APT rules actually opens them up to even larger PSR breaches when they are charged for 2018/19-2025/26.  Whoopsie!
Morning  A man finds joy in giving an apt reply — and how good is a timely word! —Proverbs 15:23

The first aim was to reverse the (blatantly unfair) rule changes which required clubs to prove FMV without access to the database.  The second was to have the APT rules declared unlawful so that they could sign a monstrously large deal with Etihad and not be stopped by PL rules.  The third aim related to the second part of their defence strategy at the Commission on the 115 charges (we’ll come back to this).  They achieved the first aim with ease.  And they also managed to achieve the second aim too. They argued that APT rules were unlawful because they exempted capital contributions from shareholders, specifically in the form of loans. They argued that if a club had a rich owner with access to cheap debt, then that was a benefit from an Associated Party vs. a club without such an owner who would have to pay a commercial rate on a bank loan. They said that FMV should apply both ways. e.g., if a club had a £100m shareholder loan at an interest rate of 2% (£2m interest costs a year) but the best rate they could get commercially was 3% (£3m interest costs a year), then they have benefitted from the APT by £1m above FMV.  The Section X arbitration panel agreed and deemed the shareholder loan exemption to be unlawful. They did not say whether this invalidated all the APT rules or not at the time, and Man City asked the panel to clarify.  In the interim, the Premier League clubs voted in new APT rules that removed the exemption for shareholder loans, despite experiencing threats from Man City not to do this. Man City wanted to invalidate the rules and if they were changed before the panel made its ruling, this wouldn’t happen.  By the time the Section X arbitration panel came back with a decision that the entire set of APT rules were unlawful, they had already been updated to a new set. This stopped Man City from passing their monstrous Etihad deal.  Now, there’s a lot of misinformation and false narratives about the shareholder loans and their impact. Their impact was a few million at most and the only club who actually benefitted PSR-wise was Everton. It made no difference for any other club and was never about PSR, it was about tax-efficient capital structuring for commercial organisations.  What most people miss is this… 1., Man City had their own no/low interest shareholder loans at the time. >£230m of them. 2., The Panel hinted as hard as they could in their decision that if they’d been asked to evaluate the APT exemption of equity contributions, then they would have treated them the same as shareholder loans… but no-one asked them to so that didn’t. Had they done so, this would have devastated Man City and Chelsea who both have huge amounts of cost-free equity (billions more than any other club).  As such, Man City going after the shareholder loan exemption was never anything to do with fairness. It was just about destroying the rules so that they could get another dodgy deal through. This time, a monster.  As it happens, it’s all irrelevant now. With the move from PSR to SCR, the capital structures are no longer even considered in the rules.  But the above clarifies the false narratives Man City bots love to try and use as mud-slinging.  Now, back to the all important third aim of Man City at the Section X arbitration on APT rules…  Man City’s lead counsel, Lord Pannick, used the hearing as a Trojan horse to undermine the concept of Fair Market Value (FMV). He used six different arguments to try and invalidate the concept’s use under the APT rules. On the surface, it merely looked like another attack on the APT rules but it was not. It was an attack on the now-defunct RPT rules. The ones that applied during the period of Man City’s 115 charges.  Pannick lost though. The panel found against all six of his arguments and in doing so, actually decided that PSR were lawful and FMV essential to their function…

Refrigeration management systems across 700+ French 🇫🇷 supermarkets were compromised in October 2026, with attackers manipulating temperature and defrost controls to cause food losses at scale.  Key findings:  - The confirmed affected systems were Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland and Dixell XWEB. This is not a new threat: pro-Russian hacktivist groups Z-Pentest Alliance and NoName057(16) claimed over 20 refrigeration attacks since January 2026, mostly targeting fruit storage, wineries, and food processors across Spain 🇪🇸, Italy 🇮🇹, and other European countries. On April 26 alone, Z-Pentest claimed 10 separate hits. The attack method in each case was the same: changing temperature and defrost settings via exposed HMIs, using legitimate supervisory functions.  - Forescout's global exposure scan found 12,976 service observations across 6,017 distinct public IPs in 99 countries. The two attack paths are weak or absent authentication (only 287 of 513 pCOWeb services returned HTTP 401 responses) and known unpatched vulnerabilities. Danfoss AK-SM 800 is end-of-life since May 2021 with no patch path. For AK-SM 800A, 80% of exposed StoreView services run firmware older than 4.3.1, leaving them exposed to CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452. Copeland XWEB Pro has 23 known vulnerabilities below firmware 1.13. CAREL products carry 11 known vulnerabilities across boss, boss mini, and pCOWeb.  - Initial access methods and responsible actors in the French 🇫🇷 incidents remain unconfirmed. Manufacturer documentation for both Danfoss AK-SM and Copeland XWEB explicitly supported direct internet exposure, port forwarding, and HTTP access for remote maintenance, meaning many installations are intentionally reachable. This creates a fractured ownership model: contractors manage the refrigeration platform, facilities teams own hardware, IT manages the network path, and no single party sees the full picture.  - Beyond setpoints, devices like CAREL pCOWeb and XWEB Pro expose Modbus-readable and writable variables, widening the impact potential. Rapid successive configuration changes observed in France 🇫🇷 suggest automation, meaning attackers scripted supervisory API calls rather than making manual adjustments, and those changes can blend into routine contractor activity with no obvious alert.  For responders and operators: the audit gap here is the correlation problem. A supervisory session log may not record which setpoint changed; a controller alarm may not identify the account behind it. Hunting for this activity means correlating remote-access session timestamps against defrost schedule changes, temperature setpoint modifications, alarm suppressions, and user account changes in the controller audit log. Review NAT and port-forwarding rules for port 80 and 443 terminating at refrigeration management interfaces. Prioritize replacing Danfoss AK-SM 800 (no patch exists) and patching AK-SM 800A to firmware 4.3.1 or later. The Forescout report details the full vulnerability table by product family.  #DFIR_Radar

🎮🚨 PS5 FIRMWARE 14.20 EXPLOIT REPORTED HOURS AFTER SONY'S UPDATE  Sony released PS5 firmware 14.20 on October 21, 2026.  Within hours, a security researcher reportedly demonstrated a working userland exploit on the new firmware.  Here's what happened:  * Firmware 14.20 was released with minor usability improvements listed in Sony's official notes.  * Researcher kuzibelit reportedly demonstrated a userland entry point on the new version.  * A Remote Lua Loader was shown executing payloads, with an FTP service reportedly running on port 1337.  * The demonstration suggests researchers have found a way to execute code in a restricted userland environment.  ⚠️ IMPORTANT DISTINCTION:  This is NOT confirmation of a complete PS5 jailbreak.  Userland execution does not automatically provide kernel privileges, hypervisor access or unrestricted control over the console.  There is also no confirmed evidence that firmware 14.20 was specifically released to patch the exploit demonstrated on 14.10.  The interesting development isn't that Sony's entire security architecture was defeated in eight hours.  It's that researchers reportedly established a working userland entry point almost immediately after a new firmware release.  Turning that access into a complete jailbreak would require overcoming additional security boundaries. 🇮🇳 ⚠️ UPDATE: eMUDHRA EXITS THE GLOBAL SSL/TLS CERTIFICATE BUSINESS AFTER CA KEY INCIDENT  eMudhra's board has decided to voluntarily withdraw from global SSL/TLS certificate issuance, the company announced on Oct 22, 2026. It follows the compromised intermediate CA key incident DDW covered on Oct 20.  What the company says: • Its G1 RSA roots will keep serving customers until the transition is complete, working with browser root programs • Affected customers will get replacement certificates from partners free of cost • Revocation and certificate-status services will run until every issued certificate has expired or been replaced • A full root-cause report will still go to the browser root programs • Affected CAs were revoked within 14 hours; eMudhra says no end-entity certificates were issued from them and its infrastructure was not compromised • Digital signature (DSC), eSign, emSigner and enterprise PKI (emCA, CertiNext) are not affected  ⚠️ Analyst Note: This is the company's own account; the customer migration is a commitment, not yet completed. A CA leaving the market does not remove its intermediates from outdated trust stores, so keep OS, browser, container and runtime CA bundles updated.  Source: finance.einnews.com/pr_news/… #DDW #DarkWeb #eMudhra #PKI #TLS #CertificateAuthority #CyberSecurity #ThreatIntelligence

sample_tweets.text: Since my posts have been shared here ~30 times in the past few weeks, it seems like I'm going to be contributing to Space Karen's Ketamine Extravaganza whether I like it or not.  I don't really intend to be active here, but I'll post some of the more important cybersecurity-focused stuff, since it gets screenshotted anyway. That way, people don't have to read post a week late and out of context.

I'll be the first to admit I'm mediocre at exploit development, but I am in contact with enough extremely talented exploit developers to say this for certain:  Anyone claiming they were "easily" able to generate a working php2shell exploit with AI is either:  a) a world-class exploit developer with an extreme case of imposter syndrome.  b) currently looking at some very confident-sounding but wrong LLM output.  I'm rather certain it's the latter based on the number of AI-hallucinated exploits I've seen posted on GitHub. Threat actors are also blasting my honeypot network with "php2shell" exploits that not only don't work, but aren't even within 10,000 miles of anything to do with how the exploit actually works.  I've seen the same technique from the attached image in multiple alleged "php2shell exploits", including one on GitHub with over 100 stars. Problem is, it's not php2shell, nor is it even a vulnerability at all. It's a technique known as "session poisoning", which can be leveraged to exploit local file inclusion (LFI) vulnerabilities in PHP apps (not PHP itself).  The only thing it has in common with CVE-2026-109618/CVE-2026-109619 is they both use the "PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" feature. And mitigation advice for both issues reference setting "session.upload_progress.enabled" to "Off".  People are shoving loose details of the vulnerability into LLMs, the LLMs are keying in on the "PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" string, then generating session poisoning code that has nothing to do with the actual CVE. And because the people doing this have absolutely no idea what they're doing, they're confident enough to post their "proof of concept exploit" to GitHub and share it on social media.  So if you see people talking about "session poisoning + LFI" it's likely their LLM hallucinated an exploit based on a 2018 blog by Orange Tsai talking about a local file inclusion attack vector.  What's even worse is that "security researchers" are then using LLMs to triage these exploitation attempts, falling victim to the same hallucinations, then confirming there is ongoing mass-exploitation (there currently isn't).  The actual real exploit is very difficult to exploit, and so far I've not seen anyone successfully get it working on more than a handful of PHP version with highly-specific configurations.  LLMs are useful tools in the hands of skilled professionals, but for others, they're often just a Dunning-Kruger accelerator.

This is 100% correct when looking at it from a single-system perspective. ASLR does not create a significant barrier to successful exploitation. But when looking at it from a mass-exploitation perspective, there are a lot of hidden complexities that come into play.  Vulnerability research is one of the few fields where you tend to make more money on the right side of the law. There isn't a huge demand for black market exploits. Most of the money is in bug bounty, working as a vulnerability researcher, or selling to grey-market exploit brokers.  This means that even the smallest bit of added complexity can take a vulnerability from 'cybercriminal free-for-all' to 'unlikely to be widely exploited'.   Mass-exploitation events are almost always preceded by someone publishing fully-weaponized point-and-click exploit code. It's extremely rare for criminal groups to successfully develop exploit for higher-complexity vulnerabilities on their own, even with AI.  So, less researchers capable of exploiting the bug means less chance of a working weaponized exploit being posted online. But also, the increased difficulty of exploitation, thus increased time/effort, discourages those who can exploit the bug from giving it away for free.  There's also per-target variability (which I don't know for sure is the case with this bug). But with more complex bugs, it'll sometimes be impossible to make universal exploits. In extreme cases, attackers may need to build exploit for each specific system or software version, or each specific config, or maybe even both.  So, while it's correct that it's not hard to find an ASLR bypass, it is difficult to find a bypass that works reliably at scale. So far, most of the working exploits I've seen are limited to just a handful of PHP versions, or bruteforcing ASLR. And that makes all the difference when it comes to the risk of threat actors spraying exploits at the entire internet.  For this specific exploit, the honest answer is, I don't know. It's above my pay grade. But I'm almost 100% certain that the level of bad this will be will be directly dependent on what kind of exploits security researchers make public.

Current information I have on php2Shell:  - The RCEs requires the attacker to obtain memory addresses which are typically protected by ASLR.  - I suspect the original author (lcfr_hax) likely has a reliable exploit which leads to stable code execution.  - Most of the PoCs being posted are completely non-functional AI slop.  - There is at least 1 working non-slop exploit being passed around, but it's reliant on bruteforcing for ASLR bypass, so not particularly impactful.  - Rumor of ITW exploitation are patchy. There are attempts being seen using the non-functional leaked RCE, or variants that are config / system specific.  - Some rumors point towards a known-working exploit being used by threat actors (I've personally confirmed this specific exploit works, but the ASLR bypass technique is unreliable at best and massively limits the potential impact).  - I'd expect heavy ITW exploitation in the next few weeks based on how many people are looking at this. Though, success rates will vary heavily based on the specific exploit chain.

🚨 Two critical Linux KSMBD remote code execution flaws disclosed before fixes were available The vulnerabilities, tracked as ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549, both carry CVSS scores of 9.0 and affect KSMBD, the Linux kernel’s built-in SMB server. ⠀ ZDI-CAN-33774 can reportedly be triggered without authentication against systems running KSMBD on port 445. 🚨 eMudhra exits global SSL/TLS certificate business following weak CA key incident The Indian digital trust company says its board has decided to voluntarily withdraw from the global SSL/TLS market after eight intermediate certificate authorities were revoked because their published keys were weak. ⠀ Browser root programs also distrusted the associated eMudhra ECC root. The company says the affected CAs never issued end-user certificates, its infrastructure was not compromised and no data was breached. ⠀ eMudhra will keep its G1 RSA roots operating during the transition and replace affected customer certificates free of charge through partner providers. Revocation and certificate-status services will continue until every issued certificate has expired or been replaced. ⠀ The company says global SSL/TLS represents around 1% of its global revenue. Its digital-signature, eSign, enterprise PKI and identity services will continue operating normally. Source: https:// emudhra.com/en/press-release/e mudhra-to-exit-global-ssl-tls-certificate-business

VeloCloud Edge and Gateway products are not directly affected. Administrators should update immediately and investigate affected systems for signs of compromise. ### 1. 현재 주요 사이버보안 트렌드
최근 사이버 위협 환경은 PHP 및 Node.js와 같은 런타임 환경의 RCE 취약점을 악용한 'PHP2Shell' 및 'Node2Shell' 공격이 급증하며 웹 서버 보안에 비상이 걸렸습니다 ([TheHackerNews](https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/urgent-php-warns-of-another-unpatched.html), [이스트시큐리티 알약](https://blog.alyac.co.kr/5788)). 공격자들은 AI 기반 침투 테스트 도구인 'Artex'를 활용하여 공급망 공격을 자동화하고 있으며, 이는 기업의 보안 운영에 심각한 위협이 되고 있습니다 ([SecurityWeek](https://www.securityweek.com/china-apt-uses-ai-pentest-tool-artex-in-connectwise-attacks/)). 또한, TLS 인증서의 취약한 개인 키를 악용한 MitM 공격과 AI 에이전트를 활용한 악성 행위가 증가함에 따라, 기존의 방어 체계를 우회하는 지능형 위협이 고도화되고 있습니다 ([Unit42](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/emudhra-certificate-compromise/)).

### 2. 주요 위협 행위자 / 캠페인
- **Sandworm**: 우크라이나 물류 기업을 대상으로 Mesh Network 백도어를 활용한 파괴적 와이퍼 공격 수행 ([TheHackerNews](https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/russian-linked-hackers-used-new-mesh.html))
- **Storm-0940**: AI 침투 테스트 도구인 Artex를 사용하여 ConnectWise 공급망을 공격, 2,200개 이상의 테넌트 침해 ([DarkReading](https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/microsoft-storm-0940-connectwise-supply-chain-attack))
- **Lazarus**: 'Operation FlashHole' 캠페인을 통해 금융 보안 소프트웨어 CrossWeb EX를 악용하고 워터링 홀 기법 사용 ([Securelist](https://securelist.com/lazarus-operation-flashhole/121541/))
- **APT41**: Baton Drop 취약점(CVE-2022-21894)을 악용하여 중앙아시아 외교 기관을 타겟으로 BlackX UEFI 부트킷 배포 ([Securelist](https://securelist.com/uefi-bootkit-blackx/121539/))
- **TAG-217**: AI 기반 ARTEX 프레임워크를 활용하여 한국 금융 기관을 타겟으로 공격 수행 ([Recorded Future](https://www.recordedfuture.com/blog/tag-217-artex-south-korean-banks))

### 3. 한국 관련 위협
- **TAG-217의 한국 금융권 타겟팅**: AI 기반 도구 ARTEX를 활용한 공격 정황 포착 ([Recorded Future](https://www.recordedfuture.com/blog/tag-217-artex-south-korean-banks))
- **PHP2Shell 공공기관 대응 미흡**: 국정감사에서 KISA의 PHP 취약점 대응 실태 및 공공기관의 보안 업데이트 미비 지적 ([데일리시큐](https://www.dailysecu.com/news/articleView.html?idxno=209033))
